Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary healthcare clinics
Comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Benin predominantly use paper-based recording for patient data. Evidence from multiple sources indicates reliance on paper registers: Abt Global's PSHPA project distributed 4,000 health data registers to private facilities across all regions, implying manual entry before aggregation into DHIS2; a 2024 study in rural Bopa district references annual statistical reports and monthly data from health centers without digital mention; Enabel equipped 244 facilities (unspecified if rural) with IT for data collection, but not point-of-care patient records. National DHIS2 is used for aggregate reporting from district level, with high concordance to facility registers in some areas, suggesting paper at clinics transcribed upward. Pilots exist (e.g., some direct DHIS2 entry in one clinic, District.Team for management), but no evidence of majority rural point-of-service digital use. Barriers: poor infrastructure (power, internet), low ICT skills, funding gaps. National eHealth strategy (2017) aims for digital HIS, but rural reality lags, with paper default and digital limited to aggregation/pilots. Score 1: entirely paper-based at rural clinics.

revised_comments: Rural primary healthcare clinics in Benin remain almost entirely paper-based for routine patient data capture. National DHIS2 use is confined to district-level aggregation and to a small number of urban facilities (for example Minonkpo Clinic in Cotonou) that enter data directly; the wider USAID-funded PSHPA project instead distributed 4,000 paper health registers to private facilities nationwide for later transcription upward. A community study in rural Bopa district (Mono department) describes routine reliance on paper statistical reports with no digital point-of-care recording. As of March 2025, a digital surveillance and teledermatology tool for neglected tropical diseases remains at pilot stage in three departments (Zou, Ouémé, Plateau) and has not been deployed at facility level. Persistent barriers include unreliable electricity and internet access and limited ICT skills among rural health staff. Overall, rural clinics capture patient data on paper, with digitisation occurring only at district aggregation level or in isolated urban/pilot sites.

Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural police stations
Comments: No evidence found of digital case recording at rural police stations in Benin. As a francophone African country, rural Republican Police (merger of former police/gendarmerie in 2018) produce standard handwritten "procès-verbaux" (PVs) for complaints/incidents by judicial police officers, as per justice ministry site charging 300 FCFA per page for paper copies. No rural-specific digital case management, pilots, or IT systems identified despite searches on national police site, INTERPOL WAPIS (regional, not station-level), justice digitalisation (ID/civil, not police), and donor trainings (ICITAP capacity building, no systems). US State Dept/UK guidance describe procedures implying paper (statements, reports to prosecutor). Directorate of Information Systems exists centrally but no rural deployment evidence. Consistent with paper-based norm for rural facilities; data likely aggregated later at higher levels.

Fresh search identified a September 2025 launch of a centralised Automated Fingerprint Identification System (AFIS, WAPIS/SIPAO programme) at the Directorate-General level in Cotonou; this is a national forensic database, not station-level case digitisation, and per the metadata guidance excluding higher-level digitisation this does not change the facility-level assessment. revised_comments: Rural police stations in Benin continue to record cases and complaints entirely on paper. Judicial police officers produce handwritten procès-verbaux (PVs), with certified paper copies issued by court registries on payment of a fee. In September 2025 the Republican Police brought into service a centralised Automated Fingerprint Identification System (AFIS), developed with Interpol/Thales support under the West Africa Police Information System (WAPIS/SIPAO) programme, but this is a national forensic database housed at the Directorate-General's technical police unit in Cotonou and does not extend digital case recording to station level. No evidence indicates rural stations use electronic case management or digital records at the point of service; case files are handwritten and forwarded on paper to prosecutors and higher administrative levels.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural primary schools
Comments: Rural primary schools in Benin predominantly use paper-based systems for recording attendance (call registers), administrative data, and monitoring, as evidenced by NGO projects like AGIR in Atacora/Atlantic using paper absence tracking sheets filled weekly from registers Action Education. National EMIS exists, with INFRE producing statistical yearbooks from EMIS data focused on primary education UNESCO IICBA, but no evidence of digital entry at rural school level—likely paper collection aggregated upward. Electricity access in primary schools is only 35% (2021, up from 20% in 2016), below SSA average, with rural national access at 12% IMF. Most primary schools lack computers, especially public/rural ones, leading to low ICT literacy Southern Voice. Isolated pilots (e.g., mobile money fees in one rural secondary) do not indicate widespread PoS digitalisation. Key barriers: infrastructure deficits, poverty, low skills. National policies promote free primary education and ICT integration ambitions, but rural PoS remains paper-based, with digital at higher aggregation levels only.

revision_notes: Cited sources (UNESCO IICBA, Southern Voice, Action Education, IMF) fetched and verified; they support low rural school connectivity/computer access but do not address the national EducMaster platform. Fresh search found EducMaster/SIGE (the primary/maternelle sub-sector platform, in service for roughly three years) requires all school directors nationwide, not only urban ones, to register and continuously update learner and staff records directly on the platform, with a February 2026 ministerial directive threatening sanctions for non-compliant directors including in rural circonscriptions. This is facility-level digital administrative data capture not reflected in the original score of 1 (Entirely paper). Recalculated to 2 (Mostly paper - some digital): classroom/attendance recording remains paper-based while enrolment and staff data capture is now digital at facility level, notwithstanding rural infrastructure constraints (electricity, computers) that may require directors to use circonscription or personal devices to comply.
revised_comments: Rural primary schools in Benin now combine paper-based classroom practice with mandatory digital administrative record-keeping. School directors nationwide, including in rural areas, are required to register and continuously update learner enrolment, class lists and teaching-staff records directly on the government's EducMaster/SIGE platform, which underpins national statistics, the primary-leaving certificate (CEP) process and payroll oversight; a ministerial directive of February 2026 threatens sanctions against directors, including in rural circonscriptions, who fail to keep class-level data current on the platform. Day-to-day classroom activity, such as attendance call registers and in-class monitoring, continues to rely on paper tools, as illustrated by NGO-supported paper absence-tracking sheets used in Atacora and Atlantique. Electricity access in primary schools nationally was around 35% in 2021 (about 12% in rural areas), and most rural schools lack computers, so data entry onto EducMaster by rural directors is often constrained by infrastructure and may in practice depend on periodic access to a circonscription office or a personal device. Rural primary schools therefore operate a mixed model: routine classroom recording remains paper-based, while core administrative and enrolment data capture is digital.

Chapter Details: Status of digitalisation of records in rural facilities
Definition: The status of digital data capture in rural civil registry offices
Comments: Rural registry offices in Benin are transitioning from paper-based to hybrid systems. Traditional practice involves paper declaration vouchers completed at health centres or via village chiefs, entered into paper registers at municipal civil status offices. However, significant digitalisation is underway: the e-SIRCEV electronic civil registration system was deployed to 121 out of 164 registries by 2021. In October 2024, Benin received 2,050 mobile registration terminals from the World Bank/WURI project to enable digital birth registration directly into the National Register of Natural Persons (RNPP) and National Register of Civil Status Events (RNEC) at health facilities across all districts. In August 2025, ANIP launched a one-stop digital birth registration pilot in 10 health facilities including regional hospitals in Natitingou and Djougou, with data going directly into the RNPP and automatic PIN generation. By 2025, ANIP issued 10.5 million civil status and identity documents, with 75% of all identification procedures handled through digital channels (37% web portal, 30% mobile app, 8% USSD). However, ANIP itself acknowledges that rural areas remain underserved and are a priority for 2026. The initial point-of-service capture at rural registry offices still largely involves paper forms before digital entry, though the infrastructure for digital-first registration is rapidly expanding. UNECA rates Benin's CRVS digitisation below 35%.

Score of 2 (Mostly paper - some digital) confirmed, as the evidence continues to describe a transitional, not yet generalised, rural rollout; no promotion to a higher code is warranted until the pilot is confirmed generalised to rural registry offices.
revised_comments: Rural civil registry offices in Benin operate a hybrid model that is still transitioning from paper to digital point-of-service registration. Traditional practice records births via paper declaration vouchers completed at health centres or through village chiefs before entry into paper municipal registers, and the e-SIRCEV electronic system had reached 121 of 164 registries by 2021. Since October 2024 the WURI-Benin project has distributed 2,050 mobile registration terminals to health facilities across all districts to enable direct digital entry into the National Register of Natural Persons (RNPP) and Register of Civil Status Events (RNEC), and in August 2025 the National Identification Agency (ANIP), with UNICEF and WURI support, launched a six-month one-stop-shop pilot in ten public health facilities, including regional and zone hospitals serving rural catchment areas such as Natitingou, Djougou and Borgou-Alibori, under which parents receive their child's Personal Identification Number by SMS without needing to visit the town hall. By early 2026, ANIP reported that 75% of all identification and civil status procedures nationally were conducted through digital channels (web portal, mobile app, USSD), with 10.5 million documents issued in 2025, though the agency continues to describe rural areas as underserved and has named them a priority for 2026 once the pilot is generalised. Point-of-service capture at most rural registry offices therefore still typically begins on paper, even as digital-first registration infrastructure expands rapidly around them.
